#3143. You can change Windows settings directly from a search now – how to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview enhances the Search feature so that you can access specific settings right from a search window.

Microsoft has been on a kick lately trying to improve and enhance Windows 11, including sprucing up Search, which is now simpler, cleaner, and friendlier. And there’s another cool trick that Search has up its sleeve: Available in the Beta channel of the latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview, Search will give you access to specific Windows settings and commands. Known as inline actions, this latest skill is designed to help you directly complete certain tasks. That means you no longer need to know exactly where or how to find the setting you need.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

Curious about built-in features such as Dark mode, Bluetooth, screen brightness, Remote Desktop, the Windows clipboard, or Windows Update? Just type the name or phrase in the Search field. The results then display an Open button that you can select to go directly to the related setting.

“A new Windows Search experience built on WinUI 3 is beginning to roll out,” Microsoft said on a web page announcing the latest Insiders build. “It’s faster, more efficient, and features a streamlined design that makes results easier to scan. Inline actions let you quickly complete tasks directly. Turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust your screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange windows from Windows Search.”

I tried this with several different Windows settings, and the results window pointed me to the right screens for tweaking them. Though I know where most Windows settings are located by now, there are still times when I forget how to reach certain ones. This new skill promises to be a time saver whenever I face that challenge.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC

Here’s another handy enhancement. How often do you type a word or term in Windows Search only to misspell it? With the latest update, Search will now better understand what you actually mean and match you with the correct results. Type “drak” instead of “dark,” for example, and you’ll still see the results for Dark mode.

Microsoft promises these latest improvements to Windows Search will continue to be fine-tuned over the next few weeks. And there’s more in the new Preview build.

Ever run into trouble using Windows Hello facial recognition in a dark area? Now, your screen will temporarily brighten up to help you sign in under those conditions. To enable this option, head to Settings, select Account, select Sign-in options, and then click Facial recognition. Turn on the switch for “Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition.”

The latest Insiders build also tweaks features such as Live captions, Gaming, File Explorer, and Microsoft 365 cloud storage.

Also: How I used ChatGPT to talk me through fixing a corrupted gaming PC

To grab this update, you’ll have to join the Windows Insiders Program if you’re not already registered. You can then sign up for the Beta or Experimental channel, either of which will give you access to the new Search skills and other features. Make sure you’re running the Beta Preview Build 26320.9876 or higher. To check, go to Settings, select System, and then click About. The Windows Info section will indicate the build number.

As for regular Windows users not enrolled in the Insiders Program, the new changes should reach you relatively soon. I’d expect them to roll out with the December Patch Tuesday update arriving on December 8, so that Microsoft can squeeze them in before the end of the year.

#3141. Oracle Stock Just Surged After CoreWeave Earnings. Here's Why One Analyst Says It's Built for the Data-Center Backlash

Oracle shares rallied with other AI stocks on Wednesday. One analyst thinks Oracle is better positioned than rivals as political pushback against data centers grows.

Oracle (ORCL +8.81%) shares rose nearly 9% to about $128 on Wednesday, part of a broad rally in AI stocks after AI cloud company CoreWeave (CRWV +24.71%) raised its revenue forecast and reported a massive order backlog of about $132.5 billion.

The jump follows a brutal stretch. Even after Wednesday's gain, Oracle is still down about 34% this year and more than 60% from its record levels last year.

CoreWeave and Oracle are in the same business: renting out huge amounts of AI computing power. Both are spending heavily to build data centers, and investors have worried about how they'll pay for it.

CoreWeave's report eased some of that worry. Its CEO, Michael Intrator, said the company's growth is funded partly by "financing backed by customer contracts" and about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone. In other words, customers are paying up front for capacity they want, which suggests demand for AI computing is real rather than speculative.

That obviously matters for Oracle, which is making the same kind of bet, but on a much bigger scale.

The latest worry for AI stocks is political. After last week's midterm elections, investors grew concerned that states and towns could restrict new data center construction. The restrictions have gotten bipartisan support. On Wednesday, Sen. Josh Hawley called for a moratorium on building them.

Still, analysts at Mizuho think Oracle is better prepared than most. In a note on Monday, the firm said all five of Oracle's mega sites are already under construction, and four have the necessary permits. The firm said potential delays are already built into Oracle's guidance, and that tighter permitting could even help Oracle by limiting new AI computing supply. Mizuho called the recent sell-off a buying opportunity and kept its Outperform rating.

Oracle's own numbers show why investors care. In its latest quarterly report, for the three months ended Aug. 31, cloud infrastructure revenue more than doubled to $7.4 billion. Total revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion.

Its remaining performance obligations, or revenue it's already under contract to collect, reached $664 billion, up from $455 billion a year earlier. Oracle said the jump came mainly from "significant" (or, large) cloud contracts.

Building all that capacity costs a fortune. Oracle spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures in the quarter, more than three times the year before. That left free cash flow at negative $5.4 billion, well below negative $362 million one year prior. To help pay for it, Oracle raised about $19.9 billion by selling new shares, which, of course, dilutes existing shareholders.

Oracle is also carrying a lot of debt. It had about $125 billion in senior notes and other long-term borrowings at the end of August. There is a bright spot: like CoreWeave, Oracle's customers are paying in advance. Prepayments added about $11.4 billion to its operating cash flow in the quarter, helping that figure nearly triple to $23.1 billion. Profit is growing, too, with earnings per share up 54% to $1.56.

Oracle also expects to recognize only about 13% of that $664 billion over the next 12 months. Much of the payoff seems years away, and depends on customers following through.

Mizuho makes a good point: if building new data centers gets harder, companies with sites already underway have an edge. But Oracle is a high-stakes bet that AI demand will last for years.

At about $128 a share, Oracle is worth roughly $390 billion. For investors who believe in that story, the stock's 34% drop this year offers a better entry point. Just size the position for the risk, and watch Oracle's next earnings report in December for updates on spending and its backlog.

#3140. Can you still trust Proton?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company’s reputation took a major hit two weeks ago, when 404 Media published a detailed report, based on leaked Slack messages and interviews with anonymous insiders. The story detailed a push by Proton CEO Andy Yen to — in his own words — “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity.”

Also: Is your browser’s free VPN enough? I tested 4 against Proton VPN

After one employee proposed spending at least a few days on penetration testing before shipping new code, Yen reportedly said, “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure. Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” According to 404 Media’s account, Yen’s message for Proton engineers was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

After the original story broke, 404 Media posted a follow-up story reporting that the company had canceled its “re-interviews” that were intended to assess how developers were adopting AI. A 404 Media podcast was titled “Proton’s CEO Is Putting AI Before Security.”

Reddit has an especially active Proton community with 345,000 weekly visitors. It quickly filled up with so many comments — the majority of them negative — that moderators created a single megathread to help keep track of the different threads, including pages for general criticism, support of the AI usage, and “leaving your goodbyes.”

Also: Best VPN services 2026: Expert tested and recommended

Given the level of interest, it’s not surprising that Yen chose that forum to post a public message to the community. In it, he apologized for “hurtful” remarks, adding that he’s “determined to do better.”

He also addressed the topic of AI-based security reviews:

But most importantly, I need to categorically state that our use of AI will never be at the expense of security. In the past year, contrary to what has been alleged, actually additional layers of security review have been added to meet the threat posed by hostile AIs scanning Proton’s open source code for vulnerabilities. Fast and secure need not be mutually exclusive. We also leverage AI to find vulnerabilities in our own code before attackers do. Our code is open source, and its security remains open for all to verify. [emphasis in original]

Nothing in the 404 Media reporting demonstrates that Proton weakened its encryption or shipped insecure code because of AI. The damage is different: Yen’s remarks undermined confidence that management will consistently respect the security processes its customers rely on.

In a blog post that Proton shared with ZDNET ahead of its publication today, the company followed up on Yen’s promise to “lift the hood on how we use AI internally at Proton.” The post, titled “How Proton keeps your data secure in the age of AI,” was signed by the Proton Team and emphasizes Proton’s secure architecture, with end-to-end, zero-access encryption:

We do not hold the keys to your emails, files, or passwords, so we cannot read them, and no AI tool can, either. Our documented security governance policies have not changed since June 2024, before AI was even a major factor in our work here, and they all still apply.

On Reddit, Yen said, “AI is here, and it will unquestionably change how software is developed forever, and Proton must also change.” Today’s post clarified that code receives the same checks whether it is written by a human, by an AI agent, or by a combination of both. Every change receives automated security scans but also requires human approval; sensitive changes, such as core cryptography work, require review by specialist teams. Major feature designs are also reviewed for security, dependencies, testing, and deployment plans.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – no VPN needed

Those policies address the most serious technical concerns raised by the current controversy, although outsiders have no way to know from the policy alone how consistently those safeguards are followed in day-to-day development.

Should a modern software company use AI for security? Proton argues that it can’t afford not to.

Because of AI, attacks that once might have required a nation-state can now be executed by almost anyone. A defender relying on manual processes and hand-crafted tools is bringing a knife to a gunfight. An attacker only needs to find one flaw, while a defender needs to close all of them. AI is the only tool that makes that defense possible. Cybersecurity is an arms race, and the teams working on security at Proton have been some of the earliest adopters of AI, because the safety of your data depends on winning that race.

But that argument doesn’t really address the objection. The current controversy isn’t about whether Proton should use AI to find vulnerabilities; it’s about whether pressure for “AI velocity” can override the judgment of engineers responsible for keeping its products secure.

Proton says it uses AI to review code changes, identify vulnerabilities through continuous security reviews, and monitor an attack surface that has “grown far beyond what unaided humans could monitor.” The company uses its own models alongside non-public cyber models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The modern software development landscape is torn by two opposing forces. On one side, you have AI-based tools that are routinely finding nightmarish vulnerabilities in existing codebases and then exploiting them immediately. On the other side, you have a global movement that’s skeptical of the benefits of AI and outright opposed to construction of the data centers where they run.

Much of Proton’s growth over the past few years has been the direct result of people trying to escape big tech. So it shouldn’t be a surprise that many of Proton’s customers — at least those who are passionate enough to visit a Reddit forum — are deeply skeptical of anything related to AI.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

In a traditional software company, that realization would have led management to cautiously roll out AI-based features and reveal its AI-centric security strategy more deliberately. That didn’t happen here, obviously. Those blunt remarks from the CEO exposed a management culture that many employees and customers found troubling. It’s difficult to restore trust, both within the workforce and among customers, after that kind of public display of contempt.

Ironically, one of Yen’s comments from the original 404 Media story describes the company’s current dilemma with devastating accuracy.

In a Slack message, Yen told a Proton engineer, “perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.” The implication was that he was urging the employee to lie, or at least shade the truth. In fact, as Yen himself told a random Reddit commenter:

I do not believe perception should be more important than truth. I am stating that unfortunately it often ends up being the case. If you place it into the context in which it was said, it can be understood as, “it doesn’t matter that the truth is that Proton’s PQC implementation is better, this truth is irrelevant as long as it is not perceived to be this way, and we therefore need to correct that perception”

That’s Proton’s challenge now, distilled to its essence. It takes seconds to destroy a reputation. It can take months or years to recover from the perception that the company and its management can no longer be trusted.

Personally, I will continue to use Proton Pass and Proton VPN, both of which are solid, reliable products. But I’ve moved my secondary email accounts (which I had migrated from Gmail to Proton Mail); they’re now running on Fastmail. I had been considering making the switch for a long time, primarily because Proton Mail’s performance has been too slow for my taste. Current events just hastened that switch.

This conference call contains time-sensitive information that speaks only as of the live broadcast today, November 11, 2026. With that, it's my pleasure to turn the call over to Dikla Czaczkes Akselbrad, Chief Executive Officer of PolyPid. Dikla?

Dikla Akselbrad: Thank you, Yehuda, and good morning, everyone. We are now just over two weeks from our PDUFA goal date of November 28th, and this is a defining moment for PolyPid. Close to half of them are open procedures. We plan to initiate communications with the FDA on this work in the fourth quarter. Beyond abdominal surgery, we see opportunities in soft tissue and bone surgery. Under our current agreement with Azurity will fund the clinical development once we jointly prioritize indications. In Europe, we submitted our marketing authorization application to the EMA on September 14, meeting the third quarter timeline we had communicated.

Shortly after quarter end, the EMA validated the application and began its formal review, with a decision expected in the second half of 2027 and a potential EU launch in 2028. At the same time, we mutually agreed with ADVANZ PHARMA to terminate our 2022 agreement for Europe, and the exclusive European commercialization rights to D-PLEX100 have revert back to us. We now fully control our European strategy, and we are in active discussions with potential commercial partners. In Canada, part of the Azurity collaboration, a new drug submission is planned for 2027.

To summarize the milestone ahead, our PDUFA goal date in two weeks' time on November 28th, the start of FDA communications on broader abdominal surgery this quarter, the U.S. launch of D-PLEX100 in early 2027, subject to approval, the NTAP decision in August 2027, and in the second half of 2027, the EMA decision, as well as the PD01B pre-IND meeting and first-in-human study. It brings reach, more than 10 hospital-administered products, more than 200 U.S. commercial-facing colleagues, and the GPO contracting and institutional relationships that reach more than 1,700 leading U.S. hospitals and academic centers. It also brings relevance, a hospital-prescribed antibiotic on the market that gives it credibility with infectious disease specialists and bowel preparation products used by the same colorectal surgeons D-PLEX100 will initially serve. We see the commercial launch of D-PLEX100 as a process that will build over several months, starting in early 2027. In a late-breaking oral presentation by Dr. George Viola of MD Anderson Cancer Center, an exploratory pooled microbiology analysis of our clinical data covering 2,185 patients looked at infections that occurred despite prevention. The finding from the abstract added microbiologic context to the SHIELD II results. Dikla Akselbrad: Feel free to add to that also based on the latest conference. Couple of things that we are hearing from colorectal surgeons in particular, and those are very detailed into the data that we show in our phase III. What they really get from this data is obviously the 60% reduction of infection. That is obvious. That is the key secondary, and this is easy for them to know that they have a certain percentage of surgical site infection in these patients. It is shown to be reduced by 60%. The other thing that they do, they look at, they also look at the. Those are, of course, open procedure.

The other thing that they mentioned to us, and this was coming almost from everyone that we spoke with, is the fact that the bottom line of our incident of surgical site infection with D-PLEX was lower than what they see in their minimally invasive business. Ori Warshavsky: Sorry, I was on mute. I was on mute. I would just add that surgeons, before they go into these procedures, they assess the patient based on risk. Again, what D-PLEX does is help reduce some of this risk and mitigate this risk. This is kind of how they triage the patient, and this is how they prepare. I think this is what they will gain most from, or when they think of where to apply or where to use the product, it is really based on the risk assessment.

We know from literature, we know from data that risk factors, smokers, diabetics, high BMI, older patients have higher risk for infection, and this will be kind of the target for the product.

Chase Knickerbocker: Got it. Maybe just last from me. Any kind of conversations as part of this review that kind of give you a sense for how FDA is thinking about kind of the bar for you on label expansion, particularly into broader abdominal surgeries? Thanks.

Dikla Akselbrad: We discussed this briefly on our R&D Day about two weeks ago, but also in our prepared remark today. This is ongoing. So the expansion from colorectal to abdominal, this is a work that is internally on the motion, and we said that we plan to initiate those discussion with the FDA this quarter. So you can imagine that the package to the FDA is up and ready. We will be submitting it this quarter. I think it's premature to discuss what the requirements will be before we actually hear from the FDA. But we think we have a very good case to expanding from colorectal, and specifically from these broad phase III data to abdominal.

But let's wait until we hear from the agency.

Operator: Your next question comes from Jason Butler from Citizens.

Jason Butler: Hi. Thanks for taking the questions, and congrats on the progress. Two questions. Maybe a quick follow-up to the label expansion question. Given the funding commitment from Azurity, how quickly do you think you can start to look at surgeries beyond abdominal surgery? Is that something that could even happen in parallel, or do you expect it to be a sequential process? Then second question, Dikla, can you maybe just comment a little bit more about your expectations for the ramp in adoption throughout 2027, and to what extent is the or how important will the NTAP be to driving adoption? Thank you.

Dikla Akselbrad: Sure. Good morning, Jason. So, we are prepared and ready, and label expansion is very important both for Azurity and to us. This is one of our major levers of growth. We've discussed this very detailed, looking at PolyPid into 2030. We view this as the most, or maybe I shouldn't say the most, but one of the most rewarding expansion that we could pursue around D-PLEX100. This is the same way that Azurity looks at it, and it was important for them to have the ability to expand to other surgery. This is why it is covered with our mutual agreement.

To tell you whether things could be running in parallel or one after the other, it won't be smart to go into that when we have an FDA discussion, or we are initiating a discussion very soon. I think this is something we'll need to comment once we hear the feedback. But presumably, there are specific surgeries or specific area that could be done in parallel. I'm not sure if this is the best way to do things in parallel.

It could be in a specific area within the area of abdominal and soft tissue, but maybe there are area where we first need to see or to build a strategy with the FDA to convince them that after having additional safety data, additional proof, this could be done. We'll also need to see how this is adopted in the market to the sense that we'll hear from surgeons, we'll hear from hospital, where they want to see this next. So I think this is also something that is important. Ori, you want to touch the second question about the NTAP?

Ori Warshavsky: Yeah, I'll take it. Jason, good morning. You had two questions on ramp-up and NTAP. First on the ramp-up, the plan is really once the product is approved early 2027 to start with launch activities. Launch activities mean that the MSLs are out there to the target hospitals, finding those champions, the surgeons that can bring the product to P&T. Then P&T needs to review, get additional input from their economic assessment, from the quality pay folks, from the infectious diseases specialists. Then after this review, an update to the electronic systems to be added to formulary. It's a process that takes a little bit of time, and it's a process that is done really account by account.

Some hospitals are reviewed, the P&Ts convened every month, and some every quarter. Some of the IDNs review hospital by hospital, and some do one review for the entire network. We will see over the next several months, accounts coming in a sense, in a stepwise approach. One quarter there'll be a set, and then the next quarter will be either more or less, depending on the cadence within the hospital. Without really giving a I know I'm not giving you a specific date, but it will a process that will take several months until we start really seeing traction. It connects also to the NTAP.

When we ask in market research, we ask pharmacists that lead P&T committees about the willingness to put the product on formulary and in stock, there was very high, close to 90% willingness to put the product on formulary. Then we asked them, "Okay, how would the NTAP change your answer?" The answer was, "Okay, from 90% this would go to 100%." They would want to see the data holds without NTAP, meaning the pharmacoeconomic data holds without NTAP, and then NTAP comes in as an addition just kind of to make the decision easier to accept. Timing-wise, it'll be, so if the NTAP application was submitted, it will be approved in August, so and in effect next October.

Really, as P&Ts complete their assessment and ready to put the product on the formulary and for surgeon to use it, NTAP will be there active and ready to go.

Dikla Akselbrad: Hi. Good morning. Thank you for that. I would say like that. Obviously, as a matter of practice, the FDA is part of the NDA review. It is a standard process that the FDA conduct a preapproval inspection of our manufacturing facility. But I think that at the stage that we are, as a matter of practice, we should not comment on any specific labeling and timing status of preapproval inspection. We said in the press release that everything has been either set to support the regulatory milestone or has already been done. PDUFA is in just about two weeks. I think we have to be patient.

We are standing behind everything that we said, both in terms of the timing and the label discussions that are underway. That by itself is a strong signal to where the review process is. We'll need to be patient a little bit more.

Boobalan Pachaiyappan: That is super helpful. Thanks for that. In terms of Azurity, trying to do all the pre-launch activities. I am just curious whether they are finding out hospitals where there is very low baseline infection rates or operatives with more intensive prevention protocols, because in those cases, the economic case for D-PLEX use could be a little bit more challenging. Dikla Akselbrad: Sure. I will start, and Ori, please add on. They are looking first on First, you need to remember that Azurity has a pipeline of products around mechanical bowel prep. They are speaking with the colorectal surgeon now on a daily basis, and they have their KOLs and the surgeon that they are frequently in contact with. They also have our KOL that has been with us along the development and during the clinical studies. They are the first candidate for approaching. Those are the ones that they are looking at to reach out to first. Ori, you want to add to that something?

Ori Warshavsky: Yes, I think, that is the first step. The second step is, and this is really in line with how we saw the market, is really to go to the academic centers where guidance are written. What I heard when I spoke to some of the surgeons in the academic centers is really, it is almost kind of a race to who has the best technology. If you do not adopt a new technology and your peer across the street does, and they now show better results, or they have something that is more interesting that patients coming in, they kind of compete on the same patient.

Although in some of these academic centers, the infection rates are maybe lower than in some of, let us say, general hospitals or community hospitals, they do have interest to bringing the newest technology, the most effective one, and they are competing between themselves on what to use and how they are measured compared to other top hospitals. That is the kind of the next level of target hospitals that Azurity is looking at.

Operator: Your next question comes from [indiscernible] Larsen from Oppenheimer.

Unknown Analyst: This is Jeevan on for Les. Thanks for taking our questions. First one is, when should we expect pricing disclosure? What net cost per procedure are you discussing with the hospitals, and maybe how that compares with the expected savings from preventing infections? Then, follow-up is, does FDA approval alone trigger the Azurity milestone, or are there other label conditions attached to that? When would the cash be received, and when would that revenue be recognized?

Dikla Akselbrad: Welcome. In terms of the pricing, Azurity will share the pricing at the launch. This is obviously their decision. I can say that up until now, everything that they've learned is very much in line with what we have seen. We obviously shared with them our past market research. Some of the highlights of those were disclosed by us in the past, but this will be their part to disclose. Ori, you want to add anything to that?

Ori Warshavsky: No, that's how it is. The pricing will be decided ultimately by Azurity.

Dikla Akselbrad: As for the second part around milestone, around approval, so as everyone probably recall, we received already $30 million, and there are over $290 million in development, regulatory, and sales milestone. We did not disclose the breakdown of these over $290 million between the three. What we did say is that the development and regulatory milestone are all relatively in the short term. Other than that, I can't really add much to that.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your question comes from Brandon Folkes from H.C. Wainwright.

Brandon Folkes: Maybe just one multi-part from me. How much health economic benefit data do you envision hospitals to require for uptake initially? I know you had generated some good health economic data in the past. So does that still hold for launch, or do you anticipate having to generate new or updated data for the hospitals? Along those lines, do you expect some of the hospitals to run their own experience trials before broad adoption? How large of an investment into post-approval real-world data are you and Azurity contemplating? Thank you.

Dikla Akselbrad: Ori, you want to take this one?

Ori Warshavsky: Yes, I'll take it. Hey, Brandon. The data that we have, we believe is sufficient for launch. This is from our conversations. We've shown, just as Dikla mentioned earlier, we've shown a reduction in the severity of infection, a reduction or a delay in the onset of breakthrough infection, which is very important to the hospitals, because if the patient is discharged, then the whole economics change. We've shown a reduction in length of stay overall for the hospital. So, we believe we have sufficient data for what is needed to demonstrate the economic case in front of P&T. Now, we also had conversations with a number of hospitals regarding your question on, let's call it, the pilot study.

The overall consensus is that if there will be a need for a pilot study, it will be a small handful of patients, seven to 10 patients, something on this level, really to check how the surgeons are comfortable with the product. It wouldn't be an efficacy study, but more really to understand the usability and how it works with the workflow of the operating room. So, that is something that is expected, that is something that Azurity is looking for. Beyond that, the post-approval kind of real-world data, I think it's a little bit early to discuss. In any case, it will be part of the tactics of Azurity on how they drive demand in the market.

But of course, we will support them with our data as needed.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's question and answer session. I will now hand back for closing remarks.

Dikla Akselbrad: Thank you all for joining us today and for your questions. With our PDUFA goal date fast approaching, Azurity preparing for launch, our MAA under review in Europe, and advancing PD01 development, we look forward to updating you on our progress in the weeks and months ahead. #3137. How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New research provides a stark look at the AI supply chain and the risks it brings to businesses.

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a new wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a new report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite says that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate users and email, and address network security issues.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

Enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs

It’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security issues.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.

#3136. Google Introduces 3 More Top-Level Domain Names, Including .Eat and .Fly

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Prospective website owners can now register domains geared toward food, travel and local bands.

We’re trained to type .com almost on autopilot, but more top-level domains are coming. You’ll soon see websites ending in .eat, .fly and .here. It’s a new way for restaurants, travel agencies and other service providers to customize their online presence.

Google successfully filed these domain types with ICANN, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, back in 2012, but only released the new registry options to the public on Tuesday.

There’s always a concern that someone will steal a business’ domain name, a process known as cybersquatting. To prevent new top-level domains from being registered and ransomed at high prices, Google’s partnered registrars offered .eat, .fly and .here websites to registered trademark holders ahead of a wider rollout. This closed access period lasted from Sept. 1 to Nov. 9.

Google’s blog post about the new domains revealed several big businesses that have already secured new web addresses during the trademark holder selloff. Wingstop bought up wingstop.eat, while agriculture and food-tech company Clayton Farms secured the america.eat address. Caddy, Canary and Voltair are some of the businesses with new .fly domains.

The most interesting assortment of companies have tied down .here addresses. In its blog, Google describes .here domains as denoting businesses “where people get things done.” They utilize fairly common words that people might search for. Real-estate app Zillow owns rent.here and sell.here, while bloodtest.here is owned by SiPhox Health, a home blood-testing service.

A number of Google-partnered registrars are now accepting registrations for the three new domain types.

There’s currently a one-time early registration fee associated with registering the new domain names, though it is diminishing and will completely disappear on Nov. 17. After that, any currently unused .eat, .fly and .here names can be registered and maintained at a fixed annual rate, just like any other type of domain.

A representative for Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Bose has issued a recall of more than 670,000 lithium-ion battery packs used in the company's S1 Pro and S1 Pro+ Bluetooth speaker systems due to overheating issues.

According to a Consumer Product Safety Commission announcement, Bose has received reports of the battery packs overheating to the point of melting, producing smoke or catching fire. Fortunately, no injuries have been reported.

The recall specifically affects battery packs that include any one of the following six digits in the serial numbers: 083723, 078352, 084105, 078591, 078592, 084106, or 086409. You can find the 17-digit number on the label printed on the bottom of the pack.

These packs were sold both with the S1 Pro and S1 Pro+ speakers as well as accessories, for between $100 and $160 from December 2017 through July 2026. The speaker systems cost $700.

In total, 634,759 were sold in the US, with an additional 35,400 in Canada.

If you have the S1 Pro or S1 Pro+ Portable Bluetooth Speaker Systems, Bose requests that you stop using the battery packs immediately and remove them from the speakers. You can still use the speakers connected to AC power.

If you have an uninstalled battery pack, you just need to find the serial number and send it to Bose.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Bose is asking owners to register and provide the serial number at http://www.bose.com/support/s1-battery-recall. The company is providing a free replacement battery pack.

You'll need to dispose of the battery safely, which means do not just throw the battery pack in the trash or in used battery recycling boxes at retail or home improvement stores. Lithium-ion batteries must be disposed of differently from other batteries because of the greater risk of fire.

You'll need to look up your local municipality's household hazardous waste collection center. You should contact the center because not everyone accepts lithium-ion batteries. They will generally be able to point you in the right direction.

#3134. Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Alongside the Ring Drone Cam, Ring introduced the Rover Cam for businesses. It investigates disturbances and streams 4K footage.

Today, Ring announced the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both new robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

The Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

That makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

There’s one other very important caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other issue).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

The Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

The other product Ring announced is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

If another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

Even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.

#3133. MiNK Therapeutics (INKT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

First revenue lands as the ARDS trial enters randomized Phase II.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

MiNK Therapeutics, Inc. (INKT +2.14%) reported its first pre-commercial product revenue and the strategic advancement of its cell therapy platform across critical illness and oncology. Management detailed the launch of a named patient program for agenT-797, which allows for physician-directed access outside of clinical trials in multiple countries. The company transitioned its lead program into a randomized Phase II trial for ARDS, with ongoing enrollment in Ukraine and planned activation at U.S. clinical sites before the end of the year. Financial operations were focused on prioritizing spend for this randomized readout while utilizing non-dilutive funding sources, including a multiyear agreement with ARPA-H and various investigator awards.

#3132. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for solid returns

The Federal Reserve indicated the possibility of a rate hike this year after its latest meeting, which could have implications for income-seeking investors.

Given this backdrop, dividend-paying stocks with strong yields and upside potential could help investors earn attractive returns.

Backed by solid research, top Wall Street analysts can provide key insights to pick stocks having the ability to generate compelling capital appreciation and pay consistent dividends, driven by solid fundamentals.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Kinetik is a midstream company operating in the Delaware basin. With a quarterly dividend of 81 cents per share (annualized dividend of $3.24 per share), KNTK stock offers a dividend yield of about 7%.

RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and increased her price target to $53 from $50, citing expected growth from the KL2 project and sour gas opportunity in New Mexico. Scotto updated her estimates to reflect Kinetik's Q1 2026 results, with adjusted EBITDA beating estimates, driven by improved margins and Gulf Coast marketing gains that offset Waha price-related shut-ins.

The five-star analyst expects the Waha price-related shut-ins to persist until incremental takeaway capacity comes online later this year. Scotto said that Kinetik is well-positioned to capture New Mexico sour gas growth prospects when prices support activity. She sees the Northern Delaware Basin in New Mexico as a major growth opportunity for Kinetik. Scotto highlighted that Kinetik has purpose-built its system for sour gas handling, giving it an edge over new competitors that may face permitting delays of at least three years to build acid gas injection wells.

Additionally, Scotto pointed out Kinetik's attractive capital return framework, which targets a 3.5x to 4.0x leverage ratio, 3% to 5% hike in annual dividend until dividend coverage reaches 1.6x, and opportunistic share buybacks.

"We still view KNTK as a logical takeout candidate for buyers seeking to increase equity NGL barrels and sour gas processing," said Scotto.

Scotto ranks No. 211 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 16%. See Kinetik Financials on TipRanks.

Oilfield services company SLB (SLB), formerly known as Schlumberger, is this week's second dividend pick. The company announced a quarterly cash dividend of nearly 30 cents per share, payable on July 9. At an annualized dividend of $1.18 per share, SLB stock offers a dividend yield of 2.5%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on SLB stock with a price target of $63, saying that he believes the company is "positioned to capitalize on long-term opportunities in oilfield activity globally triggered by the ongoing disruptions and shifting supply dynamics in the Middle East."

The five-star analyst expects SLB's dominant position in the international oilfield services market to bolster its earnings power over the long term, supported by increased activity levels over the medium to long term.

Given management's commentary on accelerated exploration activity in regions such as Latin America, Africa and Asia, and his expectation for accelerated final investment decisions in deepwater projects in West Africa, the Gulf of America and Brazil, Mehta expects SLB to benefit from higher services activity needed amid increasing drilling and production.

#3131. Half of New Games on Steam Are Now Made With AI. How Does This Reflect the Gaming Industry?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of those games are unpopular, with 10 or fewer reviews from gamers.

Steam, the digital marketplace for PC games from game studio Valve, has hit a major milestone, sparking pushback from parts of the gaming community: Approximately 50% of new Steam games in October were made with the help of AI.

This underscores a growing trend in gaming, where more games are made with some form of AI assistance — specifically, generative AI, which developers have used to generate code, art assets, voice lines and more. Developers are adopting the technology in increasing numbers.

The numbers come from a Reddit user who goes by Ploz, and who used Steam’s publicly available data to see how many newly released games relied on AI in some capacity. This was possible because of Valve’s AI disclosure policy for newly released games, which requires developers to state whether they used AI in making their game. The disclosure is part of the storefront’s publicly accessible records, allowing anyone to view it.

A Valve representative did not respond to a request for comment.

The data is a snapshot of the tidal wave of AI-made games flooding storefronts, most prominently Steam. But crucially, Valve has chosen not to limit this flood, washing its hands of the problem and leaving gamers to fend for themselves in finding quality games. Developers had already been struggling to get their games noticed, and Valve’s limited curation seems completely unprepared for the firehose of AI-made games churned out on an increasing scale.

Valve implemented the AI disclosure policy in January 2024 to increase developer transparency. At the time, only 1.4% of newly released games used AI. This increased to 13.4% by the end of 2024, then to 24% by the end of 2025. It now sits at 49.9%.

There are some caveats. The AI disclosure is only required for games that use AI to create player-facing content, such as artwork, sound, character dialogue and localization. The 49.9% figure is specific to these types of games and doesn’t account for developers who use AI for behind-the-scenes tasks such as coding and bug fixes. A Google Cloud survey conducted in August 2025 showed that 87% of developers use AI for backend work, which doesn’t require disclosure on Steam.

So it’s likely that the number of games on Steam built with AI assistance is greater than 50%. Ploz notes that the only way users can avoid AI-generated games is to manually check for AI disclosures.

According to Ploz, the most common use of AI in game development is for artwork, which was mentioned in 63% of disclosures. Text and translations gobbled up 30%, while music (21%), code (16%) and voices (7%) rounded out the list. Many developers had more than one of those areas named in their disclosure, and about a quarter of developers said they were using AI for their Steam store pages and marketing.

About 3% of developers used AI directly as a game mechanic. One such example is a driving simulator called Teach My Little Sister How to Drive. Developers use AI in the game to interpret a player’s voice commands and generate the sister’s responses. To keep a playable demo of the game available to the public, the development team, Easy Fox, is paying $1,000 every day just to cover these AI operating costs — an expense so high that it was forced to take out a loan simply to keep the demo running.

For development, there are loads of options. The Unity 6 engine came out in October 2024 and includes AI code assistance, AI asset generation and third-party integration with Claude Code, Gemini and Grok. Anthropic’s Claude is a fairly popular option among smaller developers, since it supports the ability to vibe code whole games, with ChatGPT, Gemini and GitHub Copilot as other options.

Many of the games being released with the AI disclosure on Steam can be classified as slop — a derogatory term gamers have applied liberally to titles that heavily lean on generative AI for development and look derivative of other popular games. According to Ploz, most AI-enabled games are small: Around 47% of new games with fewer than 10 reviews have an AI disclosure. Among developers who released more than 10 games in a year, 68% of those games included the disclosure.

Games with AI disclosures received fewer positive reviews on average than those without. And among all newly released games with more than 1,000 reviews, only 17% include an AI disclosure. That means gamers are still gravitating toward games without an AI disclosure and pushing back against games that use the technology.

Developers seem aware of this. CNET reached out to two dozen well-known developers, including Epic Games, EA, Activision Blizzard, Ubisoft, PlayStation Studios and many others. All of them declined to comment.

Bigger studios may be using AI in their development, but it’s hard to tell the scale. There’s no such thing as an AI audit yet, and the industry seems to be relying on voluntary disclosure for now. Steam’s disclosure policy has outed smaller developers who are either worried about violating the policy and being taken off the digital storefront, or aren’t worried about the negative effects of disclosure.

A lot of dominoes had to fall for this to happen. The availability of AI tools and the increasing ease of use are definite contributors. Subreddits like r/AIGameDev have plenty of examples of people putting together games with just a few days or weeks of vibe coding, which is a lot shorter than the standard video game development cycle, which can stretch over years depending on the scale, production level and graphics quality. This practice has exploded over the last couple of years, resulting in a lot of games getting launched that are made mostly or entirely with AI.

Many of these games end up on Steam, which doesn’t have a policy limiting AI-developed games.

“Digital storefronts like Steam have already struggled to moderate low-effort and poor-quality games, as well as copycats stealing other games’ ideas,” said CNET Managing Editor David Lumb.

Valve openly admits its role in this, stating that the problem definitely exists but that the company doesn’t “want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn’t use.”

It takes a similar stance on AI cloning, with Valve’s Tom Giardino telling developers that “you must continue to grow your game by adding features, personality and creativity that stem from your own perspective as a developer.”

These policies essentially allow any AI-developed game or clone to reach the Valve storefront without pushback, which certainly contributes to the flood of newly released games with some form of player-facing AI involvement in their development.

Rival store Epic Games has a similar stance, allowing basically any game that wants to be there. The company declined to comment further about this, but CEO Tom Sweeney is an avid supporter of AI in video game development, stating that it was “perfectly logical” for developers to rely on AI to handle the mundane grunt work that takes up most of a developer’s time.

While Steam and Epic Games tend to take a more lax attitude toward AI slop, other storefronts like Itch.io are not. Itch.io has a whole policy against AI slop and the company has willingly, and at times gleefully, deleted terabytes of AI slop from its storefront. It also requires developers to disclose if they used AI but takes a much more consumer-friendly approach by letting users filter those out of search results if they don’t want to see them.

Some measures are being taken to address the proliferation of AI slop, but none will entirely stop the problem. Cloning has been a problem for many years. Mobile gamers of a certain vintage may remember the flock of Flappy Bird clones that appeared on app stores after the original game went down, and those weren’t even made with AI.

AI makes cloning much easier and faster, and some AI companies are addressing it. Anthropic recently changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games. Anthropic engineering leader Addy Osmani posted on X that using Claude to copy games infringes on intellectual property rights and violates Anthropic’s policy.

However, during CNET’s testing, we found we could still make games resembling popular titles, so cloning remains possible with a little creativity.

“This has come up over and over on the subreddit r/GameDev, and there’s no real solution if Steam and other digital storefronts don’t stem the flood of low-quality AI games drowning out the labors of love that entertain and innovate,” Lumb said.

Many developers openly oppose AI and refuse to use it in their own work. However, as the Steam stats show, that crowd’s output appears to be getting smaller and smaller every year amid the unending stream of AI games.

#3130. 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

With the latest betas for iOS and other platforms, Siri AI is now available to all developers for full integration into their apps. Here are the ones I hope will jump on board.

One of the many benefits of the new Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade

With App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the new developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now

“Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple said in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the new and full Siri AI integration.

I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”

Right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV shows, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are currently available to borrow.”

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in New York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”

As my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Asking Siri to tackle those tasks would certainly be a time saver. I could ask it to “find the closest Italian restaurants using Yelp and show me ones within a one-mile radius that have earned four stars or higher.”

With App Intents, Siri AI can already handle advanced, complex, multi-step tasks for built-in apps. With all developers now able to take advantage of this same support, I’m expecting a lot of apps to jump on board. Let’s hope my favorites end up on the list.

#3129. Drug Makers or Biotech Bets: Which ETF Is the Better Buy, State Street’s XPH or First Trust’s FBT?

One fund holds about 60 drug companies at a lower fee. The other holds 30 biotech names and has a stronger long-term record. Either way, expect some volatility.

State Street SPDR S&P Pharmaceuticals ETF (XPH +1.31%) provides broad, low-cost exposure to the pharmaceutical industry, while First Trust NYSE Arca Biotechnology Index Fund (FBT +1.28%) offers concentrated biotechnology exposure with a history of higher returns.

Investors seeking targeted exposure to the healthcare sector often choose between biotechnology and pharmaceuticals. Both funds track life sciences companies, but they differ in their degree of concentration, sub-sector focus, and expense structures, providing distinct risk-reward profiles for those looking beyond a broad healthcare index fund.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

The SPDR fund is more affordable than its counterpart, with an expense ratio of 0.35%. This is 20 basis points lower than the 0.55% fee charged by the First Trust fund.

State Street SPDR S&P Pharmaceuticals ETF allocates 100% of its portfolio to the healthcare sector and currently holds 62 positions. Its largest positions include Veradermics (MANE +5.47%) at 2.86%, Xeris Biopharma Holdings (XERS +4.36%) at 2.76%, and Pacira Biosciences (PCRX -0.08%) at 2.51%. The fund was launched in 2006.

First Trust NYSE Arca Biotechnology Index Fund also focuses exclusively on the healthcare sector but maintains a much more concentrated portfolio of 30 holdings. Top positions include Genmab (GMAB -0.37%) at 4.89%, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (REGN +4.73%) at 3.95%, and Halozyme Therapeutics (HALO -1.26%) at 3.77%. The fund was launched in 2006.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

Healthcare has been making plenty of headlines lately, from the boom in GLP-1 weight-loss drugs to a busy stretch of biotech acquisitions. For long-term investors heading into 2027, the State Street SPDR S&P Pharmaceuticals ETF (XPH) looks like the better way to play it. It costs less than First Trust's biotech fund, holds roughly 60 companies, and pays a small dividend.

XPH is not a big-pharma fund, though. Its equal-weight approach gives smaller drug developers as much influence as the giants, and it has taken deep drops in the past. That makes for a bumpier ride than the name suggests. Still, owning twice as many companies as FBT means one failed trial hurts less, and the smaller names give it room to run when bigger drugmakers come shopping.

FBT owns about 30 biotech companies in equal amounts, has the stronger long-term record, and pays no dividend. It works best as a smaller add-on for those seeking additional biotech risk. XPH's lower fee and broader lineup make it the better core holding for most long-term investors.

#3128. We’ve Folded the iPhone Duo Almost 400,000 Times. How Much More Can It Take?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Our Fold-a-Phone machine folds Apple's iPhone Duo 900 times every hour to test the durability of its hinge.

We’re now a third of the way through November, and the machine in CNET’s lab continues to work overtime testing Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this poor phone more than two weeks ago, and since then its only job has been to bend and flatten, bend and flatten, until it breaks.

So how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 3 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10, we’re at 390,000 folds, and by tomorrow we’ll reach 400,000 folds.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. Over the last week, I’ve seen a lot of chatter about the sturdiness of the Duo’s folding hinge and its potential to fail or crack. I’ve periodically examined the Duo we’re testing in our machine, and so far, I haven’t seen any signs of damage. And the crease isn’t any more visible than it was when we took it out of the box. If that changes, I’ll let you know here and on our livestream.

In the meantime, let me explain what we’re doing. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.
