#3127. Reddit launches AI-powered Reviews feature – with 10,000 products to start

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Reddit is adding AI-generated product reviews that compile real user sentiment from across communities. Here's how they work.

If you regularly turn to Reddit for product advice, your experience is about to change.

Reddit announced a new feature on Tuesday called Reddit Reviews, which takes conversations from subreddits across the site and compiles them into AI-generated, in-depth product summaries. The feature works much like Google AI Overviews and is likely an attempt to better compete with them.

When you search for a product on Reddit, you’ll see an “easy-to-digest format” that has a “what people are saying” recap. A visual breakdown will show whether conversations are generally positive, mixed, or negative, as well as common sentiments among users. If you want to go deeper, Reddit says you can browse comments about a product, apply topic filters, read original user discussions, ask follow-up questions, or explore other commonly compared products.

In an example shared by Reddit, a user searches for “Best headphones 2026.” The search returns several results with tags like “Very positive,” “Positive,” and “Mixed.” Clicking on one expands to a review that says, “Reddit likes the XL224’s fantastic battery life, powerful bass, and strong sound quality, while the steep price and fit on smaller heads draws criticism.”

“A mix of generative AI and other in-house technology” is used to identify themes and summarize what people are saying, a representative explained, and added that “the technologies and models we use may evolve over time to best support the experience.”

Perhaps the most important part is that Reddit Reviews are shaped by users, and companies can’t pay to have product features. For a community sensitive to commercialization, this is a big deal.

My first concern was about bots or other fake reviews, but a Reddit representative said they’re taking that into consideration. “Platform-wide,” the representative said, “we are labeling apps and prompting accounts we detect to be running automations to either verify there’s a human behind the username or be labeled as an app.” In this context, an app is a registered API client that’s developed to interact with Reddit (including posting, commenting, upvoting, and scraping). In short, the system will label known bots.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep watch – even upstairsSpecifically for reviews, a “review conversation” will appear that describes a person’s experience with a product. Reddit also has “defined rules,” it says, “to help our LLMs identify these review conversations based on the surrounding conversation for context.”

You’ll start to see Reddit Reviews over the next few weeks in the US on iOS, Android, and browser versions of the site. Around 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel will be available to start.

I find myself frequently adding “reddit” to Google searches for everything from the best restaurants in a city to the best headphones for my kids, so these overviews are definitely intriguing. It’s not easy right now to wade through numerous threads, so if this does make it easier to get true user sentiment, it could be a big plus.

#3125. Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next – 7 reasons why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

After using a Debian-based distribution, you may find yourself longing for something different. I know exactly what you should try next.

Back when I was constantly distro-hopping, I found it important to have a “what’s next” mentality. That way, I could plan accordingly, instead of jumping in blind. I could prepare myself for the installation, the package management system, the desktop, and other necessary bits and pieces.

Also: Fedora Everything let me build the Linux desktop I actually want

But more than anything, I always found it best to know which type of distribution should be next.

You wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to, say, Gentoo, as the leap in required skills is considerable. You also wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to Debian, since Ubuntu is based on Debian, making it a lateral move. From my experience, when coming from an Ubuntu-based distribution, the best next distro is one based on Fedora.

This statement wouldn’t hold water five years ago because Fedora often required work to get it running properly. Now, Fedora requires no work or effort to get it working out of the box. Hardware support is on par with Ubuntu, modern boot processes are supported, it has an excellent first-boot experience, Nvidia driver support is out of the box, the touchpad works out of the box, suspend and resume work flawlessly, it ships with a newer kernel, it includes built-in support for modern display stacks, and it’s clean and bloat-free.

Like many Linux distributions, Fedora lets you choose your desktop, but it does so better by offering dedicated spins for each. You’ll find Fedora spins for KDE Plasma, Xfce, Cinnamon, Mate-Compiz, i3, LXQT, LXDE, SOAS, Sway, Budgie, Miracle, Plasma Mobile, and COSMIC. Instead of manually installing your desktop of choice, just download the Fedora spin with your desired desktop.

Also: Fedora 44 made me forget I was using Linux – in the best way

Yes, there’s a Debian-based distribution for every desktop, but knowing you can just go to the Fedora Project Spins page and quickly find what you’re looking for makes the process easy. As well, Ubuntu has its own “flavors” (such as Kubuntu, Lubuntu, etc.), so coming from an Ubuntu flavor will make total sense.

When using a Debian-based distribution, if you install/manage software from the command line, you’re used to APT, such as sudo apt install quillmark. Did you know that Fedora’s DNF works in the same way? That’s right: sudo dnf install quillmark will get you the same results as sudo apt install quillmark (so long as the app is found in the Fedora repositories).

The same holds true for removing software. One difference, however, is that when system software is upgraded, you’ll have to reboot a Fedora-based distribution for the upgrades to take effect. The only time you have to reboot on a Debian-based distro upgrade is if the kernel is upgraded in the process.

If you’re using Ubuntu as your Debian-based distribution, you’ll find that it includes a universal package manager, just as Fedora does. On Debian, the package manager is Snap, while on Fedora it’s Flatpak. While these two are different, they do have some similarities, such as app installation.

Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why

With Snap packages, the installation goes something like this: sudo snap install quillmark. On Fedora, that command would be flatpak install quillmark. You’ll notice that sudo is not used with Flatpak; the reason for this is that Flatpak apps are typically installed on a per-user basis. Yes, you can install them system-wide, but that defeats the purpose of sandboxing.

Both Fedora and Ubuntu are secure, even if they arrive at that security by different routes. For example, Ubuntu has AppArmor and Fedora has SELinux. However, both of these tools manage Mandatory Access Controls — just in different ways. The good news is that you’ll probably never have to touch either system.

Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: After years of testing both, here’s my verdict

Also, both Debian- and Fedora-based distributions tend to ship with a GUI frontend for the firewall. If you don’t find one installed, you can install one through your package manager. It is important to know that the Fedora firewall manager is considerably more powerful than Ubuntu’s, which also means it has a steeper learning curve. The good news is that, out of the box, you probably won’t have to make many changes to the firewall, other than ensuring it’s enabled.

Once upon a time, I would have debated such a statement, but Fedora is now on par with Ubuntu in terms of user-friendliness, especially if you choose one of the more user-friendly spins (such as KDE Fedora, Cinnamon, or MATE-Compiz). Fedora also has a System Settings app similar to Ubuntu’s; each one lets you manage nearly every aspect of the computer, so there’s no need to use the command line with Fedora (unless you want to).

With Debian, the release cycle is every 2 years, and support is 5 years. With Fedora, the release cycle is every 6 months, and support is 13 months. If you’re using an Ubuntu-based distribution (which is based on Debian), the release cycle is the same as Fedora, but there are two versions: LTS and interim. LTS support is considerably longer than interim releases: LTS releases receive 5 years of free support, while interim releases receive 9 months.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

In the end, the Fedora release/support cycle is faster and simpler.

Because both development teams focus on building a user-friendly distribution out of the box, migrating from a Debian-based to a Fedora-based distribution is seamless. When making such a transition, aside from a few minor differences, you’ll feel like you never left your Debian-based distro, especially if you choose a Fedora Spin that includes the same desktop you’ve been using.

Time's running out for some Versa and Sense models. After Nov. 28, you can no longer install or update third-party apps or clockfaces on these Google smartwatches.

If you have a Fitbit Versa or Fitbit Sense smartwatch, you’ll soon be unable to update the third-party apps on these devices. Google announced on Monday an update to its older lineup of devices that may signify the beginning of obsolescence. Users can no longer install or update third-party apps or clocks on these Fitbit smartwatches, beginning on Nov. 28.

Also: Google’s Fitbit Air is a $99 screenless wearable that I can actually take seriously

The apps will continue to work after that date, but if users delete any of these apps, they will not be able to reinstall them. The changes affect the Fitbit Sense and Fitbit Sense 2, as well as the Fitbit Versa, Fitbit Versa Lite, Fitbit Versa 2, Fitbit Versa 3, and Fitbit Versa 4.

Google noted that users will still have access to Fitbit- and Google-developed apps and clocks, and that they should update to the latest app versions to keep those apps functioning properly.

The Nov. 28 support cut-off comes right on the heels of this season’s Black Friday sales. (Google’s Pixel Watch 5 just got a $100 discount at Amazon.)

So the smartwatches aren’t dead — they can still perform the same primary functions, like recording workouts or receiving or responding to messages and calls. Still, the news is a downer for Versa and Sense users who’ve been using their smartwatches and the many third-party apps on them for anywhere from two to eight years now.

All signs point to these devices being slowly phased out in favor of Google’s latest lineup of fitness trackers and smartwatches.

Also: Google’s new Fitbit Edge solves my biggest gripe with the Pixel Watch

Within the past few years, Google has unveiled an impressive new lineup of health trackers, including the screenless Fitbit Air, the screened Fitbit Edge, and the Pixel Watch 5. For those looking to ditch their Versa or Sense, a few affordable options exist in the ecosystem to take their place.

The earliest and most recent Fitbit Versa models were launched in 2018 and 2022, respectively, and the first and last Fitbit Sense models launched in 2020 and 2022, respectively — making the oldest of these devices eight years old.

#3121. Apple’s iPod Turns 25: Here’s the Song Catalog That Rode Wit You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

On this day in 2001, Apple's iconic MP3 player was released. And now, an Apple Music easter egg lets you experience the nostalgic sound and scroll of the gadget's click wheel.

Back in 2001, some of the top songs included Nelly’s Ride Wit Me, Fallin’ by Alicia Keys and Ms. Jackson by Outkast. When people wanted to listen to those songs but weren’t near a car stereo or their home audio equipment, most carried music with them on skip-prone portable CD players, boomboxes or maybe even a homemade mix cassette.

Sure, some early adopters were already carrying a small collection of songs on a portable MP3 player (MP3s: the new-new thing!) like the Diamond Rio or Creative’s Nomad Jukebox. But these weren’t common, and you didn’t see them that often. There was no ubiquitous sign yet that the times were changing musically in a digital direction.

Enter Apple in November 2001 with its original iPod, a small hard drive encased in smooth white plastic that could stash between 1,000 and 2,000 songs, a sum that seemed godly at the time.

Who would ever need to listen to 1,000 songs (or have access to that many) at their fingertips? What mortal would dare?

The iPod, which was announced on Oct. 23, 2001, and released on Nov. 10, 2001, had a starting price of $400. It heralded the smartphone era before smartphones were a thing, making portable electronics more tactile, user-friendly and information-forward. The white earbuds that were bundled with the device were the beacon of that era. Before long, it seemed everyone had white cables coming out of their ears.

For the 25th anniversary of Apple’s game-changing music player, the device’s creators are getting nostalgic about its silver anniversary. On Apple Music’s website, you can find at its 404 Not Found page a playful mockup of the OG iPod with its pleasing-to-use scroll wheel and a selection of songs you might have had in your iPod at some time or another.

CNET writers and editors had a good time playing around with the fully functional iPod online, sharing favorite hits from its music library and enjoying some nostalgia ASMR.

We also looked back at CNET’s earlier write-ups, including one from CNET’s former Editor-in-Chief Connie Guglielmo, explaining what it was like to watch Steve Jobs introduce the iPod. There’s also a great 2021 piece by CNET’s Scott Stein on the iPod’s evolution, and a commentary by CNET’s Ty Pendlebury on how the iPod captured and held the throne for so long, surviving music streaming and rival players.

Read more: iPhone Duo Review: Late to the Foldable Party, but It Steals the Show

If the iPod can be primarily credited to one person — leading a team of many — it’s widely acknowledged to be Tony Fadell, who came to Apple as a contractor and went on to head one of its most successful product divisions. These days, Fadell is thinking a lot about the future of AI assistant devices, but he took time on his LinkedIn to acknowledge the iPod anniversary this week.

“We took it from approval to shipping in less than eight months,” he wrote. “There wasn’t time for endless refinements. We had to make decisions, trust our experience and stay focused on one clear promise: 1,000 songs in your pocket.”

While Fadell says that the iPod took a few generations to really take off and eventually come in iterations like the Nano and the Touch, some music fans who still love the original iPod design have been using the device for decades. If you have any hard drive-based gadget that lasts that long, count yourself lucky.

In addition to those old enough to remember what a Hoobastank is, iPods are also getting popular again with younger generations on a nostalgia kick, many of whom would rather carry around a separate physical device for their music than stream their Spotify accounts on their phone for the millionth time. Axios reports that iPods and MP3s are back in a big way in a trend called “friction-maxxing.” You don’t have to use that term to indulge, we promise.

Getting into the hobby isn’t cheap: Working iPod models can cost several hundred dollars on eBay. And one that’s never been opened? Try $25,000 to $60,000.

A cheaper route may be to keep the familiar outside trappings but replace the guts with a new motherboard. A group called Crowd Supply promises in a YouTube video a new way to bring nonworking iPods back to life. It hasn’t launched yet, but you can keep an eye on the project at Crowd Supply’s website. Other tinkerers have had years and years to work up hundreds of iPod hacks; you can find many of them on Hackaday.

Alternatively, it may be the function that a modern MP3 enthusiast seeks, not necessarily the Apple branding or hardware. Other companies, such as Fosi Audio, have their own takes on the modern music player, like the $80 DAP Neo. CNET has a list of the best MP3 players of 2026, with devices like the Shanling M0s and the Android-based HiBy R4 coming out on top.

Lastly, if you want to relive the iPod glory days, you don’t necessarily need new (or old) hardware at all; your phone can do it with iOS apps such as RetroPod, My Classic – Retro Console or, if you’re feeling saucy on Android, ClassiPod.

#3120. Evolution Petroleum (EPM) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Asset sales and a new Permian deal are shaping debt reduction and buyback plans.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Evolution Petroleum Corporation (EPM -3.64%) reported fiscal first quarter results that were centered on the integration of its $16 million Permian minerals acquisition and the conversion of nonproducing acreage into cash through farm-outs. Management reported that revenue increased 6% year over year as higher realized commodity prices offset unplanned downtime in legacy working interest assets. The company is prioritizing a capital allocation strategy that emphasizes the growth of high-margin mineral and royalty interests, which do not require company-funded drilling or completion costs. Management stated that near-term financial priorities include utilizing asset monetization proceeds to reduce debt while sustaining the quarterly dividend and evaluating potential share repurchases.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Evolution Petroleum Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Earnings Release Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Brandi Hudson, Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Brandi Hudson: Thank you. Welcome to Evolution Petroleum's Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Earnings Call. I'm joined today by Kelly Loyd, President and Chief Executive Officer; Mark Bunch, Chief Operating Officer; and Ryan Stash, Senior Vice President, Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer. We released our fiscal first quarter 2027 financial results after the market closed yesterday. Please refer to our earnings press release for additional information containing these results. You can access our earnings release in the Investors section of our website. Please note that any statements and information provided in today's call speak only as of today's date, November 11, 2026, and any time-sensitive information may not be accurate at a later date.

Our discussion today will contain forward-looking statements of management's beliefs and assumptions based on currently available information. These forward-looking statements are subject to the risks, assumptions and uncertainties described in our SEC filings. Actual results may differ materially from those expected. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statements. During today's call, we may discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures, including adjusted EBITDA and adjusted net income. Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in our earnings release. Kelly will begin with an overview of the quarter and our strategic priorities. Mark will follow with an operational update, and Ryan will review our financial results and liquidity.

Kelly will then provide closing comments, and the management team will take your questions. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. A webcast replay will be available in the Investors section of our website. With that, I will turn the call over to Kelly.

Kelly Loyd: Thank you, Brandi, and good morning, everyone. There's a lot to talk about this morning, and I'm pleased to say most of it reflects real progress on our strategy. During the quarter, we closed on a $16 million Permian minerals acquisition, expanded our Haynesville and Bossier Shale royalty position in Louisiana. And after quarter end, we continued our strategy of turning undeveloped acreage into cash. Revenue from the quarter was up 6% from a year ago. Production was slightly up from the fourth quarter. Adjusted EBITDA increased from last quarter. And while net income came in at a loss for the quarter, it was due in large part to hedging losses, most of which were noncash.

Beyond just the quarter's headline numbers, we're very excited about the progress we're seeing across important parts of our business, particularly our mineral and royalty portfolio. September production from our newly acquired Permian interest has already exceeded our acquisition expectations and new wells in Louisiana are beginning to contribute just as we expected. We bought these assets for both their existing production and their substantial development potential, which is really beginning to deliver. What makes that development particularly valuable to us is how it is funded. Our operating partners bear the drilling and completion costs, and we receive our share of production without having to make those additional capital commitments.

We also do not bear lifting expenses on these mineral and royalty interests. That means growth in these assets contributes high-margin cash flow without the CapEx associated with working interest development. As these contributions continue to build, it gives us more capacity to strengthen the balance sheet and further support our dividend. Specifically in the Permian, from the effective date of August 20 through September, production averaged approximately 218 barrels of oil equivalent per day, ahead of the 200 to 210 BOE per day we expected. We have sufficient production data to include the results from 21 of the approximately 27 gross wells that operators brought online between closing and September 30.

That September rate does not yet include production from those roughly 6 additional wells that we know are online. In our fiscal second quarter, we expect to benefit from a full quarter of ownership, production from those 6 wells and production from new wells that come online during the quarter. It's exciting to see this level of activity so soon after closing. Our Louisiana interest offer a similar opportunity. Production from our Haynesville and Bossier royalty interest grew approximately 92% from the fourth quarter as operators brought new wells online, very much in line with our expectations. We added a couple of small bolt-ons during the quarter and have continued adding to the position since quarter end.

We've been building this position over time, and we are now seeing this acreage begin to contribute in a meaningful way. We are also looking beyond new production for ways to realize value within the portfolio. We own a great deal of undeveloped acreage with meaningful long-term potential. Like we did in the fourth fiscal quarter when we sold minerals for $3 million that we felt were unlikely to be developed in the next year or 2, we always consider the best path to bring value forward to today across our portfolio, whether that's participating in development through working interest, selling longer-term development prospects or farming out the acreage to a partner, we have many ways to accelerate value.

In the right situations and where the operator is aligned with us, a farmout of working interest with an override and/or an option to participate can be the most efficient option. It allows us to bring in cash today and retain an interest in future production with 0 CapEx net to us. Following quarter end, we did farm out some undeveloped acreage in the Williston Basin for approximately $2.5 million while retaining a 0.25% overriding royalty interest. This acreage represents roughly 2% of our roughly 40,000 acre position and just a fraction of the 300-plus probable and possible drilling locations that we have identified.

We're also in negotiations for further farm-outs of very low or noncurrently producing acreage here and in other parts of our portfolio that we hope to be able to report on soon. These agreements are expected to generate cash upfront and overrides and possible options to participate, and we intend to apply these proceeds to pay down borrowings on our revolver. That gives us a way to reduce debt while keeping today's production and cash flow fully intact. We expect to find more opportunities like these as we work to strengthen the balance sheet and create value for our shareholders while maintaining future upside. Taken together, these opportunities shape how we are allocating capital.

We've already invested in assets that can contribute more as they develop, and our near-term priority is to realize those returns in the quarters and years ahead. With meaningful growth already built into the portfolio, we can be highly selective about new capital and put more of the cash we generate towards strengthening the balance sheet. That approach also supports our dividend. The Board has declared a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, our 53rd consecutive quarterly payment. And since December 2013, we've returned approximately $156.6 million to shareholders. When we think about that commitment over multiple years and across commodity cycles -- and the growth underway in our mineral and royalty portfolio strengthens our ability to support it.

For fiscal 2007 7, we're off to a start that really reflects the portfolio we've been building, new production from our Permian and Louisiana interest, value emerging from undeveloped acreage and a clear path to stronger cash generation. We look forward to updating you on that progress next quarter. With that, I'll turn the call over to Mark for more details on our operations.

J. Bunch: Thanks, Kelly. Good morning, everyone. I'll focus on the development activity and operating performance across our portfolio and what we see as we move through fiscal 2027. Overall, first quarter operating performance was up sequentially. Underneath that, the picture varies by area. So let me take them in turn, starting with SCOOP/STACK. At SCOOP/STACK, new well activity continued across both our working interest and mineral and royalty positions. During the quarter, 2 gross wells came online, 8 gross wells were in progress, and we elected to participate in 3 additional gross wells. In Louisiana, new wells continue to come online across our Haynesville and Bossier mineral and royalty interest.

During the quarter, we acquired approximately $300,000 of additional interest, primarily in undeveloped acreage that third-party operators are actively developing. That activity continues to build our production without requiring us to fund drilling or completion costs. In the Permian, integration is progressing well. As Kelly mentioned, operators moved at least 21 gross wells into producing status between closing and September 30. With additional wells entering production and a full quarter of ownership, we expect a larger contribution in the second quarter. For now, our Permian and Louisiana volumes are reported within TexMex and other -- and as they become more established in our reporting, we plan to present their contributions separately.

At TexMex, operating costs declined compared to the year ago quarter following the change of operator. In the Barnett Shale, we have met with the new operator whose entire focus is solely on Barnett operations and improving field profitability through operating changes and workover opportunities. At Delhi, oil production was affected by continued compressor downtime during the quarter. Finally, at Chaveroo, we continue to work with our partner on the timing of future drilling. We view the development inventory as attractive, particularly in the current price environment, and we'll provide updates as plans develop. With that, I will turn it over to Ryan.

Ryan Stash: Thanks, Mark, and good morning. As Brandi mentioned earlier, we issued our earnings release yesterday, which contains more information on our results. For today, I'd like to go through our fiscal first quarter financial highlights. In fiscal Q1, production averaged 6,978 BOE per day, up 1% sequentially and down 5% year-over-year. The lower year-over-year production was due to unplanned downtime at our Delhi and TexMex assets as well as natural declines across the portfolio. In addition, the prior year period includes flush production from wells brought online at Chaveroo Field. These declines were partially offset by development in our SCOOP/STACK asset as well as mineral and royalty acquisitions in the Haynesville/Bossier Shale and Permian.

Total revenues were $22.6 million, down 7% sequentially and up 6% year-over-year. The sequential decrease reflected lower realized oil and NGL prices, partially offset by higher natural gas realizations and increased production. Compared to the year ago quarter, average realized prices before hedge settlements increased 11%, more than offsetting the decline in production. Net loss for the quarter was $3 million or $0.08 per diluted share compared to net income of $4.6 million in fiscal Q4 and net income of $0.8 million or $0.02 per diluted share in the year ago period. The quarter included a $4.1 million unrealized loss on derivative contracts compared to a $5.8 million unrealized gain in fiscal Q4.

Excluding selected items, adjusted net loss narrowed to $0.3 million from $0.6 million sequentially compared to an adjusted net loss of $0.1 million a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA increased sequentially to $6.8 million, driven by lower operating costs as a result of increased mineral and royalty production that helped offset lower revenues. Compared to the prior year quarter, adjusted EBITDA declined from $7.3 million, primarily due to lower production and lower realized natural gas prices compared to the prior year period. Lease operating costs decreased to $12.4 million compared to $13.1 million in the year ago quarter.

The decrease was primarily driven by lower operating costs at SCOOP/STACK and at TexMex following the change of operator as well as lower taxes and gathering and transportation costs associated with decreased natural gas prices at Jonah and Barnett. On a per unit basis, LOE per BOE improved approximately 1% from the year ago quarter and improved approximately 5% sequentially to $19.25 from $20.35 in fiscal Q4. On the hedging front, we have continued to add hedges to comply with our credit facility covenants. Our ongoing goal remains to reduce commodity price risk and protect cash flow for our shareholder return strategy while preserving the maximum potential upside.

This strategy can result in realized and unrealized losses on our hedges in some periods, but benefit us in other periods and provide more predictable and stable cash flows over time. Currently, we have hedged approximately 73% of expected PDP oil production and 76% of expected PDP natural gas production for the remainder of calendar year 2026. For calendar year 2027, we have hedged approximately 72% of expected PDP oil production and 67% of expected PDP natural gas production. Volumes for 100% of our NGL production and development on our asset base remains unhedged to provide upside to commodity pricing. We continue to utilize a mix of swaps and collars to hedge both oil and gas.

For the quarter, realized losses on our derivative contracts were $1.3 million compared to realized gains of $0.9 million a year ago. That change reduced adjusted EBITDA by approximately $2.2 million year-over-year. The volumes and prices by instrument and period are included in the hedge schedule in our earnings release. Turning to the balance sheet. Cash on hand totaled $3.1 million at September 30, down from $6.1 million at June 30. Borrowings under our credit facility increased during the quarter to $60 million from $56.5 million as a result of the Permian Minerals acquisition with $0.8 million in letters of credit outstanding and a weighted average interest rate of 6.48%.

Total liquidity at September 30, including cash and available borrowing capacity was approximately $15.3 million. We generated $8.4 million in operating cash flow before changes in working capital during the quarter compared to $6.5 million in fiscal Q4. Capital expenditures incurred were $0.7 million, and we completed the $16 million Permian Minerals acquisition. We also received approximately $12.5 million of net proceeds from our common stock offering and had $3.5 million of net borrowings under our credit facility.

Subsequent to quarter end, our borrowing base was redetermined at $70 million, down from the interim $73 million borrowing base established in August to provide liquidity to complete the Permian Minerals acquisition, but up from the spring 2026 borrowing base value of $65 million. As of October 20, availability on the facility was $9.2 million. This does not include approximately $2.5 million in cash received for the closing of the initial Williston farm-out transaction in November or any subsequent farm-out transactions that we're currently pursuing. During the quarter, we paid $4.9 million in common stock dividends.

The Board has declared a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share for fiscal Q2 2027, payable December 31 to shareholders of record on December 15, marking our 53rd consecutive quarterly payment. As we move through fiscal 2027, our financial priorities remain focused on maintaining liquidity, managing leverage and deploying capital where we expect attractive returns per share. The growing contribution from our recent mineral and royalty investments that don't require any CapEx, combined with expected farm-out proceeds support our focus on reducing borrowings while continuing to return capital to shareholders. I'll now hand it back over to Kelly for closing comments.

Kelly Loyd: Thanks, Ryan. As we move through fiscal '27, our focus is on realizing the returns from the portfolio that we have already built. We're encouraged by the early performance of our recent investments and the opportunities ahead, while recognizing that the measure of our progress will be the cash those assets generate for shareholders. We will remain disciplined in how we commit capital with debt reduction and sustaining our quarterly dividend at the forefront of our decisions. We appreciate your continued support of Evolution and look forward to updating you on our progress. I just want to say thank you and Happy Veterans Day to all of our bests out there.

With that, I'll turn it back over to the operator to begin the Q&A session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question today comes from Jeff Grampp with Northland Capital Markets.

Jeffrey Grampp: I want to start on the Permian. I know it's super early here, but just curious how the performance thus far has been relative to the underwriting model. I know you guys were expecting that asset to grow, and it seems like that's playing out. But just kind of curious how that's tracking in early days. And if you have a rig count on the assets, that would be interesting as well.

J. Bunch: So Jeff, it's Mark Bunch. And so far, like at the rate we're converting, it'd be almost like we'd be converting it around 200 wells per year. So we're actually really quite happy because we actually didn't underwrite on anything that large. And I'll let Ryan answer the question about the rig count.

Ryan Stash: Yes. So we're still -- Jeff, we're still running 8 rigs currently out there. Double Eagle has got 4. Exxon's got 4. The other interesting thing is even since the end of the quarter, we've seen upwards of 30 to 40 permits actually been filed here since the end of the quarter. Diamondback actually filed some new ones on our acreage here in the last couple of weeks. And Apache still got a few out there. So we definitely think even beyond Double Eagle and Exxon, there should be some other guys moving rigs in soon.

Kelly Loyd: Yes. Jeff, this is Kelly. I mean one of the things, right, we only want to include production that we actually know, right? So we got information on 21 wells that were converted. We have another 6 that we know are on production, but we didn't have information on. So we couldn't include any results from those. So that 218 could be a little understated, frankly.

Jeffrey Grampp: That all sounds really good. I appreciate the details. For my follow-up, kind of a bigger picture question. You just have a slide in the new deck, I think kind of targeting like 20% pro forma cash flow coming from minerals and royalties. Just kind of curious, like based on this quarter's results or maybe looking forward a couple of quarters, like where does that trend over time given that the royalty stuff seems to be the faster growing of the asset base today?

Kelly Loyd: Yes. And you sort of put the nail on the head. You said today, right? So as we currently speak, I do think we continue to see some highly accretive opportunities there. So look, just naturally, with a couple of the assets that's growing and a couple of having natural declines, it should grow just on its own without us doing anything else. So we do see that growing over time. But also, look, with where we are right now, the competition for dollars to pay down debt, we'll talk to the Board about maybe even a share buyback, it gets pretty stiff. So any new acquisition is going to have to look really good.

Ryan Stash: Yes, Jeff, I don't think -- the 20% number, I think, obviously, we still feel good about, and we're probably close to that. Obviously, going forward, some of it is going to depend on performance of legacy assets versus drilling pace in the Permian, right? So we still think kind of that 20% number right now kind of makes sense, but obviously, something to change as we see how the other assets perform.

Operator: The next question comes from Jeff Robertson with Water Tower Research.

Jeffrey Robertson: Kelly, to follow on your previous discussion, from a high-level perspective, how much exposure or organic growth exposure do you think the minerals portfolio gives to help offset natural declines on the legacy non-op working interest assets and again, with the minerals interest adding volumes at 0 CapEx and virtually 0 LOE?

Kelly Loyd: Right. Well, we -- if you model it out in a static sense, it gets a large part of the way there. I don't know that it gets all the way there. A lot of it will depend on are we starting from this level with the legacy assets and the working interest assets and what they produce and how are they going to perform. So it's -- a couple of the assets didn't perform as we might have wanted. We think we have some real fixes in -- certainly in the TexMex area. And with Delhi sort of remains to be seen with more compressors were down during the quarter.

And so you just don't know what exactly it's going to do from there. But I think overall, we're pretty excited, and it goes a long way towards holding production flat without any additional CapEx.

Ryan Stash: Yes. I mean I think as we've said in the past, I mean, given the delta on production from buying royalty assets versus working interest, just where we sit today, you could see production decline some, but cash flow is going to remain pretty strong, right? So obviously, depending on strip, we do think that the addition of the assets can certainly go a long way to replacing the cash flow loss from decline in our legacy assets.

J. Bunch: Right. That's more how we look at it really is what is the cash it's going to produce.

Jeffrey Robertson: On the Williston farm-out, did the operator give any indication of their commitment toward drilling the wells that they purchase?

Kelly Loyd: Yes, the new operator, yes, they have actually have to have -- it's written such that they're required for a drilling commitment. So yes, everything is -- that well is on their drilling schedule. Jeff, I'm glad you brought that up. I mean that's something we're really excited about. If you recall, when we first bought this, there were 350-ish plus identified locations that were probable, possible sticks on a piece of paper. But for the right sort of drilling cost and for the right commodity price environment, those are very real possibilities.

And a bigger company with a continuous drilling program that can get these drilled at much more efficient cost than we and our small partner up there, they start to make a whole lot of sense. And we've seen activity, as we mentioned in the past, moving towards us. And it's allowed us to be part of a bigger group here and retain that override as well as get some cash upfront. And I think we alluded to this, we have 40,000 acres in that area. This was 636 -- and I'm excited to see what comes down the pipe as the activity and results come in. And we're talking to others that have approached us.

And to the point, like as we make other deals in the future here, they'll always have a drilling commitment associated with them, especially if we have like an override because obviously, why would you keep an override if you didn't sell out and had no recourse. So there's always going to be some sort of drilling commitment when we make one of these farm-out deals.

Jeffrey Robertson: So you can convert long-dated drilling development activity into the mineral and royalty portfolio after they drill the wells and you collect on your overrides?

Kelly Loyd: Yes. And also just allows for the fact that we're not completely selling out of our acreage. If they, for some reason, like not to drill or perform, then our acreage comes back to us. But we just don't want to disappear. We want to -- we only want it to become -- shall we say like it convert to an override if the case is they actually perform and drill wells.

Jeffrey Robertson: In the Barnett market, have the conversations with the new operators started to lead to any proposals on activity? And do you think that there will be CapEx dollars spent in that area in 2027?

Kelly Loyd: I don't know about the CapEx side, but they've already approached us about wanting to do some additional workovers. I think they've already put some online in some of the areas that were more struggling economically. So -- and they've gone into some of the areas and looked at reducing costs. So yes, we're actually really happy with the way the new operator is performing.

Jeffrey Robertson: And then lastly, Ryan, on the RBL with the $70 million borrowing base and the Williston deal, it sounds like you were able to create liquidity without having any impact on the collateral value for the borrowing base since these are undeveloped locations that you've essentially farmed down and converted to an overriding cash.

Ryan Stash: Yes, that's exactly right. In fact, I think some of the ones specifically in the Williston were actually mortgage because they were just -- it was just acreage and PUDs. And to the extent that we do the same thing, I think it's going to be the same going forward, right? So we're going to be selling very little, if any, PDP or production, right, mostly just acreage or PUDs, which won't impact the borrowing base. And it could be that the cash you get upfront is worth more than the PUDs are on the books for, right?

Operator: The next question comes from Nicholas Pope with ROTH Capital.

Nicholas Pope: I was hoping we could expand a little bit on Jeff's question on potential CapEx here in fiscal '27. As you look at some of the deals with bigger working interest where maybe spending has been a little light for the last year or so. Is there any visibility into Chaveroo, SCOOP/STACK? Like I'm just trying to broaden a little bit an understanding of what might be on kind of the -- what potential might be out there to kind of increase CapEx the remainder of fiscal '27?

Kelly Loyd: Yes. So what I'd say as far as -- we'll start with SCOOP/STACK working interest. That is kind of -- we have not seen anything that would make us change sort of our current -- the way it's looked in the past. We expect it to be similar to that. And the AFEs are sort of coming in, in line with our -- the way it has the last year or so. So I think we're kind of on pace there. And as for Chaveroo, like I said, we're excited about those. We think those wells make nice returns right now. And I'll just say we're still working with the operator on scheduling when, if, timing, all that on those.

We have some permitted wells that we think are going to have really nice returns, but we're working with the operator on that. As you know, they've had a small shake up there.

Nicholas Pope: I'll make sure to ask them about it as well tomorrow on their call. Curious, sustainability of kind of where operating costs have been running. We've seen a couple of quarters of pretty decent improvement in kind of unit operating costs. Just trying to understand a little bit how much of that might be the mix changing with more royalty interest versus some more, I guess, sustainable or longer-term kind of improvements in that -- seeing that lower operating costs across the board. Like where is that coming from? Should we expect kind of the rate that we're seeing right now to be sustained over the next year?

Ryan Stash: Yes. I mean, Nick, it's Ryan. I would expect -- in fact, we hope the rate will actually come down from what we reported, right? I mean we should continue to see some improvements, as we've mentioned, sort of in TexMex as wells have come online and the operator gets to hold kind of the asset. And then as you mentioned, certainly, the royalty production having such low LOE in the $2 to $3 per BOE range compared to kind of our other assets as that becomes a bigger piece, that's certainly going to take the LOE down.

So yes, I mean, I think we were like around, what, mid- $19, above $19 per BOE, and we do think that, that level should come down over time.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The next question comes from Poe Fratt with Alliance Global Partners.

Charles Fratt: I have 2 questions. The first of which is you're talking about additional farm-outs raising capital. Can you sort of frame the potential proceeds from those farm-outs, $5.5 million over the last 2 quarters roughly. What should we -- any way to frame what the future might hold there?

Kelly Loyd: Well, I'll play this a little closer to the best because we are in talks with a few parties right now. But I'll say this. We don't want to do everything all at once because we think as results come in, it will translate into higher value later on. But you do want to do enough to get that increased activity by the bigger operators who can drill these things as part of a continuous drilling program and be super-efficient. So be a little bit of a balance there. And by the way, we're also -- it's not just Williston. We have other areas where people have approached us, too.

So I would say, hopefully, we'll have something here we can announce pretty soon that will at least clear up your immediate-term question.

Charles Fratt: And -- when you talked about stock buybacks, Kelly, it's ironic because you just issued stock for an acquisition. But what -- is there anything within your credit agreements that's holding you back here? I mean the stock is just getting crushed. And I was just wondering sort of how you're thinking about that and whether there are any structural issues that you have to contend with?

Ryan Stash: No, there's nothing from a structural issue perspective, Poe, I mean, obviously, yes, I mean we did issue stock to get the Permian deal done. But we've also announced and as you kind of asked the question, we've had some additional proceeds come in from accelerating asset sales. So when we have that cash come in, we have the options of obviously paying down debt, which may be the initial use of proceeds, but we'll also look at making investments and where our stock -- I agree with you. I think the reaction is overdone today.

But where it's trading, I mean, it's maybe buying our stock back could be our best investment of capital right now to look at creating shareholder value. So as we -- again, as we monetize some of the portfolio and rationalize the asset base, one of the use of proceeds could be potentially buying back shares, and there's nothing prohibited in our credit agreement for that.

Charles Fratt: And then just if I may, just one more. Delhi, what's the color on that? It seems to have been a thorn in your side for an extended period of time. And can you just sort of preview what the next couple of quarters look like there?

J. Bunch: Well, yes, this is Mark Bunch. So we've been advised by the operator that one of the compressors is not running. They haven't told us when they're going to have it back up and running. And what that amounts to is that they had to shut in some production in order to not have excess CO2 that they would have to flare. So we don't know from the operator when that particular metric is going to change on how they're operating the field. We're trying to figure that out when we know that. And we have better color on that, we'll let you know.

Kelly Loyd: That compressor issue led to the step down in production this quarter. So we hope that changes and gets better, but it's already down.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over for any closing remarks.

Kelly Loyd: No, I just want to thank everyone for joining us here, and that's it. Thank you.

Operator: The conference has now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.

#3119. Google’s new AI tool just proved Signal encryption really works – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With the aim of securing other vital systems, Google DeepMind plans to open-source its AlphaProof Code.

Researchers at Google DeepMind used AI to formally verify portions of Signal‘s underlying code — meaning they’ve mathematically proven that at least parts of the encrypted messaging app’s code do what they say, without errors. That’s reassuring given how many vulnerabilities AI systems have discovered in software lately, and how many people’s communications are protected by Signal’s cryptography. WhatsApp and Google Messages use the same encryption.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

DeepMind used AlphaProof Code, “a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents,” the researchers said. They added that formal verification “is the highest standard of security assurance,” but, without automation at scale like AI systems, difficult and time-consuming.

AI companies like OpenAI have been on a math-breakthrough tear as of late, in some cases solving nearly century-old math problems with AI. By computing at such vast scale, AI models can rapidly accelerate much of the manual work mathematicians do.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Using AlphaProof Code and building on earlier verification work by the Signal Foundation, DeepMind researchers divided the verification task into two camps. Humans worked with agents to identify what they needed to prove, and multiple agents running Gemini Carbon, the company’s latest model, then executed it. The agents also audited the proof and “highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human — just 1% of the codebase, a massive time savings,” the researchers wrote.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

For good measure, researchers tested AlphaProof Code’s ability to distinguish correct from flawed code by showing it two previously fixed Signal bugs, for which it produced correct proofs.

“Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth,” the researchers wrote. “It’s also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.”

Normally, researchers need to manually develop a proof to verify software, which takes much longer. That labor-intensive barrier has made formal verification a distant promised land, until now. The DeepMind team’s verification took a month to do what might normally take experts years.

DeepMind did not verify all of Signal’s code, but noted that this test is a step toward improved security infrastructure at a time when AI is disrupting the entire cybersecurity space.

Also: How to encrypt emails in Gmail, Outlook, and more

The breakthrough reiterates how deeply AI is both a massive risk for cybersecurity and an equally powerful fix. The year 2026 has been especially marked by AI-related security incidents, many of which involve agents. At the same time, companies like Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI are developing models geared specifically toward cybersecurity, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos.

Also: How to easily encrypt your files on an Android phone

DeepMind did not share any plans to release its findings as a consumer product, though the researchers are open-sourcing their code to help others with formal verification efforts. “Verifying Signal’s core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software,” DeepMind added

#3117. Pixel 11 Pro’s HiLight Will Now Light Up When Your Besties Text You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Google's new LED light is starting to flash for more than just phone calls.

Google’s HiLight LED is starting to light up for more than just phone calls and Gemini on the Pixel 11 Pro, Pro XL and Pro Fold. The multicolored light will now glow when your preferred contacts text you in Google Messages, as part of a new Pixel Drop update announced on Tuesday.

I was pretty harsh about HiLight when it debuted on Google’s higher-cost phones as a “Pro” feature. While it hearkens back to the days of the BlackBerry notification light, which is a good thing, its limitation to just lighting up in one of five colors for your preferred contacts’ phone calls or a color swirl for the Gemini assistant made the feature’s introduction feel half-baked. Third-party apps that offered way more control over the LED made this even more glaring, including support for more colors along with app-specific customizations.

Google representatives at the launch of the Pixel 11 did say that HiLight will continue to get new features, and adding text message support is the right step toward making the light more useful. Hopefully, in time this will expand to other features that the BlackBerry of years gone would light up for, like email and app notifications.

Tuesday’s Pixel Drop also brings several of the new features that debuted on the Pixel 11 over to last year’s Pixel 10, such as Rambler for improving voice dictation and Gemini Intelligence for proactive suggestions based on information shown on your screen. For that latter feature, this should mean quick links to a feature like Google Maps when discussing dinner plans with a friend.

Google’s also gearing up to release the Pixel Tag item tracker on Wednesday and announced that Google Fi is adding multi-network support to improve cellular connections.

#3116. All your Apple devices need to be patched ASAP – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security updates for iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, and Vision Pro just rolled out.

On Tuesday, Apple released security patches for iOS, iPadOS, MacOS, WatchOS, and VisionOS, which address wireless security flaws in Bluetooth pairing, AirPlay, and Messages.

According to Apple’s security notes, vulnerabilities can allow attackers to establish a Bluetooth connection without user interaction, bypass AirPlay connection rate limits, and join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Around half of these flaws were found internally by Apple, while the others were submitted by researchers.

You should update your devices now, as several generations are affected across device categories. The following software versions include patches:

Apple’s security notes list a fix for Messages to prevent attackers from remotely joining an iMessage group chat and reading its messages. According to Apple, “an authorization issue was addressed with improved validation” to fix the issue.

There was likely a flaw in Apple’s iMessage authorization logic that allowed an unauthorized user to inject themselves into a group chat roster without permission from an existing member.

Also: Your iPhone can spot scams for you with iOS 27

Another issue in Messages could allow an authorized added member to access messages within a group chat that were sent before they joined. According to Apple, the code that caused this issue has been removed.

One security fix across devices and software versions addresses an issue where a malicious actor could establish a Bluetooth connection to your device without user interaction.

Apple was not specific about which kind of Bluetooth attack this fix addresses; however, it’s reminiscent of Bluetooth Low Energy Re-Pairing vulnerabilities found earlier this year by French researchers.

This study explains how bad actors can exploit vulnerabilities in Bluetooth Low Energy pairing logic to execute one-click or zero-click impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks against unsuspecting devices, regardless of Bluetooth version or security level.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: Your favorite gadgets could expose you

The study was published in January of this year, and the researchers reported initial findings to Apple, which “[appeared] to have hardened the re-pairing logic in MacOS/iOS 26,” according to the study. It’s possible that Apple internally found another vulnerability in the same Bluetooth pairing logic, given how many devices across Bluetooth versions are affected.

According to Apple, this issue was fixed with “improved checks,” likely meaning strengthened verification steps during pairing.

Another vulnerability pertains to AirPlay, allowing an attacker within Bluetooth range or on the same network to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. This issue also affects iOS, iPadOS, MacOS, VisionOS, and WatchOS.

This vulnerability is similar to the AirBorne attack method. This report, published in 2025 by Oligo, describes how zero-click remote code execution, user-interaction bypass, denial-of-service, man-in-the-middle, and other techniques can be used to take control of a device that supports AirPlay.

However, the current security issue is likely less serious or far-reaching and was discovered internally.

For this issue, when you pair a device with an AirPlay receiver, such as an Apple TV, AirPlay-enabled TV, or Mac, it will prompt you for a security PIN to verify your device. You can only input an incorrect PIN a certain number of times before you’re denied pairing for a period of time.

Also: The new Apple TV 4K is always listening for ‘Hey Siri’

A vulnerability in this defense mechanism can allow an attacker within Bluetooth range of, or on the same network as, your device to use a brute-force attack, bypassing the mechanism that limits the number of incorrect PIN attempts, and eventually gain access to your device. There are only so many PIN combinations.

According to Apple, “a logic issue was addressed with improved state management” to fix this problem.

Adobe has been on a journey for years to turn itself into an AI behemoth, and its latest round of Firefly AI updates brings its dreams one step closer to fruition. At Adobe Max on Tuesday, the company announced a slew of Firefly AI updates focused on building out its video-editing capabilities.

Firefly is getting an upgraded video editor. Like other creative AI companies, Adobe has been building up its AI video capabilities over the past year, with video models made both in-house and by third-party AI companies. Now, the new interface incorporates the Firefly AI assistant, which is in beta, in a bigger way. There’s a dedicated ideation panel and more ways to storyboard ideas.

It’s a more feature-packed alternative to beginner or everyday video editors like CapCut, without overloading creators with all the features of professional-grade Adobe Premiere. Part of that push is integrating agentic AI, or agents that can handle editing tasks for you autonomously. And there are a lot of AI agents coming to Adobe’s programs.

That beginner-to-intermediate design is, well, by design — Adobe is aiming to lure in folks without decades of video-editing know-how with its generative AI features. It fits with Adobe’s larger goals; it wants to build Firefly for video and image editors the same way it built Photoshop — to be the “career partner” for creators.

Another new project is Firefly Design, an AI-heavy version of a graphic design program that incorporates print, motion graphics and 3D. The intelligence assistant is a big part of the interface, where you can use text prompts to come up with variations of different scenes.

There are a few new Firefly AI image tools, and their names describe their uses well: relight, retouch and edit object. These are more precise controls, keeping with Adobe’s goal of giving AI enthusiasts more ability to edit their video content. There are also new quick actions, or shortcuts, including a video thumbnail generator that’s based on your video.

And if you remember Project Graph from last year’s Adobe Max, it’s back in a public preview as Firefly Graph. This is a node-based editing system, where you can create individual “nodes” and connect them to create an entire system, or ecosystem, of content. It won’t be for everyone, but it’s aimed at creative teams who want to visualize large workflows.

#3112. I found a hidden Android tool that solves all my tiny text troubles

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

When the print on your Android display is too small to read, and the pinch-to-zoom feature isn't working as expected, try this.

How many times have you been on your phone, wanted to read something (a piece of news, a website, etc.), only to find the text is too small and every effort to zoom in doesn’t work?

Also: 7 Android accessibility features that can make your life easier

This happens quite often when I’m viewing content in the Google News app — especially in the morning, when my eyes are still in “wake up” mode. It can be frustrating. And it’s not only text. Sometimes there’s an image I need to enlarge, but for whatever reason, pinch-to-zoom isn’t working on that particular screen.

Fortunately, there’s an option you can enable to ensure you can always zoom in on your Android device, no matter what’s on the screen. The option is found in Accessibility and is aptly called Magnification. With this feature enabled, you can quickly zoom in on the screen to enlarge any displayed content. It doesn’t matter what’s on the screen or what app is showing the image, page, or text — Magnification will magnify it.

This iteration of the feature has been available since Android 15. I found it by accident while poking around the Settings page. Since then, I’ve used it quite a bit, and it’s eased my morning frustration with reading news sites.

The Magnification feature is quite simple: once enabled, a magnifier shortcut appears on the screen. Tap that button, and whatever is on your screen will increase in size. It’s really that easy. One caveat: As long as the Magnification shortcut is enabled, the button remains on your screen. You can move the button up and down or to the left or right side of the display, but if you want the feature enabled, the button must remain.

The good news, however, is that the button does fade a bit, so it’s not glaring and in your face. You can still see it, but it gets just enough transparency that it doesn’t stand out all that much.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature

Open Settings by dragging the Notification Shade down twice, then tapping the gear icon (or tapping Settings in the App Drawer). Where this is located depends on the Android version you’re using and your device. For example, on my Pixel 9 Pro, it’s in Settings > Accessibility > Magnification. On a RedMagic 12 Pro, it’s in Settings > Features > Accessibility. If you don’t find it right away, open Settings and search for Magnification.

Once you’ve found the Magnification option, tap the On/Off slider until it’s in the On position, and the Magnifier button will appear on your screen. Tap the button, and whatever is on the display will enlarge enough that you shouldn’t have any trouble reading it.

Here’s a little tip: After tapping the Magnification button, whatever’s been enlarged can be scrolled vertically, but not horizontally. Fortunately, there’s a way to ensure that you can read everything on the page.

Also: I use Google Magnifier to read tiny print without my glasses

Tap the gear icon at the bottom right of the display to open the options pop-up. On this page, tap the “Magnifier size” icon that’s second from the right. This enables a movable magnifier you can place where you need it (kind of like a traditional magnifying glass). You can also change the size of the movable magnifier (by tapping one of the other “Magnifier size” buttons) as well as the size of the text when magnified (by dragging the bottom slider).

Also: RedMagic 12 Pro is the fastest Android phone I’ve ever seen

This feature has alleviated the early-morning frustration of having to squint (even with my glasses on) to read certain news sites. Give it a try and see if it doesn’t make your Android life a bit clearer.

#3111. NASA Is Accepting Astronaut Applications for the First Time in 2 Years

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

If you have the right stuff, you could be on the next moon mission or end up on Mars.

This type of job posting happens once in a blue moon.  If you’ve always dreamed of becoming an astronaut, NASA just made space for those who meet its qualifications. On Saturday, the agency announced that it’s seeking the next class of astronauts who will journey to the moon, build the planned 2032 Moon Base and help create the systems that will enable the first Mars mission.

NASA last accepted applications in 2024. Over 8,000 people applied, but only 10 astronaut candidates were chosen. Since the 1960s, 370 people have been selected to train as astronaut candidates, and just 32 are currently in NASA’s astronaut corps.

If you want to journey into space with NASA, you have to be a US citizen, ideally with a master’s degree in a STEM field.

In addition to completing an application package that includes a long-form resume and five references, you will also have to pass NASA’s long-duration astronaut flight physical and show strong skills in communication, teamwork and leadership.

If you don’t have a master’s degree, you can meet that requirement with at least two years of work toward a doctoral program in a STEM field, completion of a medical degree or completion or enrollment in a nationally recognized Test Pilot School program.

You also must have at least three years of related professional experience. If Test Pilot School is your only advanced technical degree, you must also have a bachelor’s degree in a STEM field.

If you’re in residency training as a medical doctor, that could count toward the professional experience requirement, but training would have to be complete by July 2027.

If you’re a pilot, you could meet the professional experience requirement with 750 hours of pilot-in-command time in a high-performance jet aircraft; 1,500 total flight hours, with 750 pilot-in-command hours, in other fixed-wing aircraft; or 1,000 total flight hours, with 300 pilot-in-command hours, in a rotary-wing aircraft.

Yes, there is a job posting for becoming an astronaut. USAJOBS, the federal government’s official employment website, states that you’ll be reporting for duty at the Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston.

It also pays to become an astronaut: $164,395 per year.

Unsurprisingly, 76% or more travel is required — or what NASA calls “extensive travel.” Kind of the point of the job, though, no?

If you meet NASA’s requirements, you have until Dec. 3 at 11:59 p.m. ET to apply.

If accepted, you’ll spend about two years in training, learning robotics, leadership, lunar geology, spacewalking and more.

After completing training, you’ll become eligible for a spaceflight assignment. Until then, you’ll be an active astronaut corps member with astronaut office responsibilities. That’s more exciting than it sounds, as it could involve supporting fellow astronauts in space or helping develop a new spacecraft.

#3108. Warhammer Survivors Isn’t Much More Than a Vampire Survivors Reskin, Which Is (Mostly) OK

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Though it passes up the opportunity to move the genre into new territory, the game is a tasty, if familiar, piece of gaming junk food.

When I first heard that developers Auroch Digital and Vampire Survivors creator Luca “Poncle” Galante were working together on Warhammer Survivors, I was thrilled. A studio of Warhammer lore fiends collaborating with a solo dev who birthed a genre seemed like a recipe for success.

But having now played through most of the game’s sci-fi battles and a smattering of fantasy incursions, I think your enjoyment of this game probably hinges entirely on how many modern bullet heaven games you’ve played. If you’re looking for something that meaningfully changes the formula, you won’t find it here.

While Vampire Survivors should be respected and lauded for laying the foundations for an entirely new type of video game, it has been surpassed by newer projects that have fundamentally changed the fledgling bullet heaven genre for the better. Newer games have implemented incredibly robust progression systems, more objective-based gameplay and entirely new camera perspectives.

There’s no problem with Survivors being knocked off the pedestal it built – every developer should learn from their peers, and the oldest games will never be the most polished games (even if they stand the test of time as cult classics).

The issue is that Warhammer Survivors just feels like a massive, reskinned expansion of Poncle’s original game. Despite a striking visual identity and plenty of Warhammer-themed weapons and items, this game never escapes the shadow of Vampire Survivors, which may diminish the enjoyment of genre enthusiasts.

Auroch Digital’s stab at a bullet heaven game isn’t unique, and its thrills wear out sooner than one might expect, but I think that’s mostly OK. It’s full of charming, vibrant Warhammer-themed pixel art, and that feels like what the true appeal of Warhammer Survivors just might be. This is the type of video game junk food that keeps you up until 5 a.m. every once in a while, completely destroying your sleep schedule. It won’t go down as one of the bullet heaven greats, and it doesn’t need to.

Vampire Survivors veterans will have a sense of deja vu from the pixel art-styling and increasing enemy clusters. There’s some extra content and quality-of-life features bolted on here, but you’ll instantly know what you’re getting into.

When players start a run, they’re dropped into iconic locations from a top-down perspective in order to purge the area of ravenous xenos and chaos cultists. The onslaught of enemies grows increasingly fearsome as time wears on, with larger and more dangerous enemies joining the fray. As players dodge and defeat the alien threats, though, they provide experience points and items that exponentially ramp up player power.

Once you start getting your hands on an expanded arsenal of weaponry, it becomes obvious why Auroch Digital was the right choice for this project – it’s a development studio full of folks who obviously love the twin worlds of Warhammer, and that passion can be found in every nook and cranny of Warhammer Survivors.

The game’s visual style is striking, which is something I’ve come to expect from any Auroch Digital game – Warhammer Boltgun has richly detailed pixel art, and the development experience from those boomer shooters has translated extremely well to Warhammer Survivors’ 8-bit arcade trappings. The cost of entry is worth it just to see massive tyranid aliens and chaos space marines rendered in all their retro glory.

And the space marine power fantasy thrives here as players wield some of the most iconic space marine weapons, including gory chainswords, hard-hitting boltguns and face-melting flamers. What’s truly special, though, is how many of the game’s weapons and passive power-ups pay homage to the series’ tabletop roots – I was chuffed to see explosive D6 dice and mini figure glue, which both became a regular part of my screen-clearing builds.

One truly unique feature allows players to collect allies that wield weapons, instead of just building out a one-man arsenal. These allies trail behind the main character, which alters how players may approach hordes of enemies.

Certain characters unlock massive buffs if they continue adding allies to the party, which introduces another way to scale up damage very quickly. This doesn’t change how account-wide progression works, but it’s a new play style that shakes up the Vampire Survivors formula.

But it was when I discovered my favorite playable character in Warhammer Survivors that I started really noticing the game’s biggest weakness. I found myself enjoying the Sister of Battle’s gameplay, since she gets to wield a holy shield that repels enemies and damages evildoers who get too close with nearly constant pulses of light. As I continued to invest in this play style, I realized that this character was a nearly one-to-one re-creation of my Vampire Survivors main (Poe Ratcho, with his stinky demon-killing garlic).

It almost feels as though Auroch Digital was afraid to deviate too far from Poncle’s original vision for a bullet heaven game. The characters and weapons feel like reskins; the upgrade shop looks nearly identical, and even the in-game war chests that elite enemies drop have the same opening animation as the loot boxes from Vampire Survivors.

Warhammer Survivors is well-built, but often feels like a massive DLC for Vampire Survivors rather than a standalone game.

There’s plenty of meat on Warhammer Survivors’ bones. The Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar universes have their own progression tracks, with unique maps, characters and secrets to unlock. Survivors’ scale is remarkable – this game is probably twice as large as Vampire Survivors was when it launched from Early Access, and it could get even bigger with post-launch updates and future DLC.

If you love Warhammer and have never played a bullet heaven game before, Warhammer Survivors will likely ensnare you the same way Vampire Survivors did the rest of us in 2022. Figuring out effective weapon combinations, slaying thousands of oncoming foes and watching loot fly out of treasure chests with all the pomp and circumstance of a digital slot machine are all still surefire ways to flood your brain with dopamine.

But if you’ve delved deep into this genre and have enjoyed the immense mechanical advancements of later games, I suspect you’ll find Warhammer Survivors a bit lacking.

At its core, this is a game centered around achieving increasingly large damage numbers to defeat foes that continue to get faster and stronger until you’re overwhelmed – it’s a simple premise that can only be mastered through repetition. Yet Poncle’s award-winning formula started wearing thin for me this time around, and I say that as someone who believes the world is richer for having more action-packed Warhammer games and good Vampire Survivors clones in it.

Too many elements feel rehashed and reused (characters and weapon drops are the worst offenders), and Warhammer Survivors very quickly begins to feel like a carbon copy of a game I’d already played. Sure, it’s copying from an excellent game. But no difficulty spike or mystery is novel enough to remove my sense of fatigue, and I was left wishing there was some additional layer of progression or mechanical depth to keep me engaged between runs.

Warhammer Survivors currently commands an even higher price tag ($8) than its predecessor. Auroch Digital is making a big ask, especially since this game doesn’t benefit from Vampire Survivors’ multiple years of free content updates and DLC. Warhammer Survivors isn’t quite as expensive as its contemporary competitors, but it also lacks their innovations.

As it stands, I think this is a solid game – but as a pricey reskin, I wouldn’t recommend it over similar games like Vampire Hunters and Megabonk, unless you’re a Warhammer fan just looking for more ways to mow through enemies.

Warhammer Survivors is available now on PC, Nintendo Switch, Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, iOS and Android for $8 and is included within Game Pass subscriptions.
